title: Honouring Student Ideas
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman critiques the pedagogical strategy of 'cognitive conflict' -- deliberately inducing student confusion to trigger conceptual change -- arguing it is both psychologically unpredictable and pedagogically counterproductive. Using his experience teaching Newton's satellite physics and an anecdote about a physics professor's manipulative telescope activity, Ashman illustrates how ego-activating pedagogy causes students to dig in rather than update their beliefs. He draws a parallel to social media arguments: once a person publicly commits to a position, they defend it with rhetorical devices rather than update it. The article distinguishes between extracting misconceptions from students (risky, dignity-threatening) versus presenting them as third-party examples the class can examine together (safe, productive). Ashman's conclusion reframes 'honouring student ideas' not as validating wrong answers but as a principled decision to protect student dignity and cognitive safety while still building accurate understanding.
points: Cognitive conflict pedagogy assumes that challenging students' wrong answers triggers productive thinking, but the human response to disconfirming evidence is unpredictable and often defensive -- especially once a student has publicly committed to a position.

Once ego is activated (by being challenged in front of peers), students are more likely to dig in than update, just as social media debaters use rhetorical evasions rather than admit error -- even when they privately know they are wrong.

The physics professor's telescope trap -- where teachers were made to feel foolish for not noticing an inverted eye-chart -- exemplifies how 'gotcha' pedagogy violates the core teaching principle of making students feel clever.

Misconceptions and non-examples remain powerful teaching tools, but who supplies them is decisive: third-party examples invite calm scrutiny, while errors extracted from students activate shame and defensiveness.
Ashman's principle 'I make them feel clever and special' is not sentimentalism but cognitive strategy -- students who feel capable engage with challenge; students who feel exposed retreat from it.
quotes: Satellites are in free fall. A key insight of the genius Isaac Newton was that the force that causes an apple to fall from a tree is the same force that causes satellite motion. When I teach this, I even use Newton's thought experiment of a huge cannon to explain what is going on and I preface this by telling students they are about to cleanly and elegantly understand something that most people who have ever lived have not understood.

Once the students had committed to the rockets hypothesis, I was supposed to challenge them. Wouldn't the rockets run out of fuel? This caused bafflement and a little frustration. The technical term is that I had introduced 'cognitive conflict', a key component of supposedly constructivist teaching.

However, these students did not go on to arrive at Newton's insight. Worse, as memory faded, there was a risk that the most salient idea they would hold on to from our discussion was that rockets make satellites orbit the Earth.

'Cognitive dissonance' and 'cognitive conflict' are related ideas that describe the human response to disconfirming evidence. The results are unpredictable and not something I would build a teaching method Page 1 Article Archive -- Education & Leadership around. Indeed, when a person has publicly backed a position, it is hard for them to back down.

I have long given up on the idea that I will persuade the person I am arguing with. It happens, but it is rare. Usually, once a person has activated their ego and publicly committed to a position, they will use any rhetorical device at their disposal to avoid admitting they were wrong.

Often, non-examples, bad ideas, common misconceptions and poor arguments are useful teaching tools. However, I avoid extracting these from my students. This could be unproductive and I want my students to feel clever. Instead, these will be presented as the product of some third party that we may all scrutinise together." Page 2
